title: Aldehydes and ketones
note: The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic: a nucleophile adds to it, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide that is then protonated. Aldehydes react faster than ketones because they are less hindered and less stabilized. Strong nucleophiles (H⁻, R⁻) add irreversibly; weak ones (water, alcohols, amines) add reversibly, usually with acid catalysis.

read.title: Attacking the carbonyl carbon
text: The C=O bond is polarized, with the oxygen pulling electron density away from carbon. That leaves the carbonyl carbon electrophilic. Nearly every reaction of aldehydes and ketones begins the same way: a nucleophile adds to that carbon, the π electrons move onto oxygen, and the planar carbonyl becomes a tetrahedral alkoxide.

What happens next depends on the nucleophile. Hydride from NaBH₄ or carbanions from Grignard reagents add irreversibly, and acid workup gives an alcohol. The class of alcohol follows from the carbonyl: formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol, other aldehydes a secondary one, and ketones a tertiary one.

Weaker nucleophiles add reversibly. Water gives a hydrate, and an alcohol gives a hemiacetal. With acid and a second alcohol, the OH is lost as water and an acetal forms. Acetals survive bases and nucleophiles, so they serve as protecting groups, and aqueous acid restores the carbonyl. Primary amines add and then lose water to form imines; secondary amines, lacking a second N–H, form enamines.

Aldehydes react faster than ketones. A hydrogen is smaller than an alkyl group, so the nucleophile reaches the carbon more easily, and alkyl groups also stabilize the partial positive charge of a ketone's carbonyl carbon.
